verdict: One idea, two sets of customers. FedRAMP certifies cloud services for federal agencies; GovRAMP verifies them for state and local governments, on the same control catalog.

rows.label: Purpose
rows.a: One security certification for a cloud service that every federal agency can reuse.
rows.b: One cloud security verification that state and local governments can share, modeled on FedRAMP.

rows.label: Who Must Follow It
rows.a: Agencies must favor FedRAMP Certified cloud services where the use is in scope. Providers follow the Consolidated Rules to earn and keep certification.
rows.b: A membership nonprofit, not a law. Its site lists 72 participating government organizations.

rows.label: How It Is Assessed
rows.a: A FedRAMP Recognized assessor assesses Classes B, C and D at least once a year. Each agency still issues its own authorization to operate.
rows.b: A third-party assessor assesses Ready and Authorized, the program office validates, and a government sponsor or the Approvals Committee approves Authorized.

rows.label: What It Grants
rows.a: FedRAMP Certified, in Class A, B, C or D.
rows.b: One of four verified statuses: Core, Ready, Provisional or Authorized.

connect: Each takes the other as a start. FedRAMP’s Class A rule accepts a GovRAMP status from the past 12 months, and GovRAMP’s Fast Track reuses FedRAMP packages. Neither publishes a crosswalk to the other.
noScore: Lensatic gives no strictness score here. The two serve different governments, and a status in one is not a grade in the other.
